entries.name: Consolidated Industries (Premier) horizontal 'NOx rod' attic furnace
entries.summary: Gas horizontal forced-air furnaces made by Consolidated Industries (formerly Premier Furnace) for the California market, usually installed in attics or crawlspaces. CPSC warned in 2000 that they pose a substantial fire risk because burners and heat exchangers can fail, and in 2001 announced a recall covering about 30,000 units sold under seven other firms' labels; the roughly 110,000 Premier/Consolidated-label units had no recall remedy. The maker is out of business and the remedy has expired, so a surviving unit simply needs replacing.
entries.date_notes: Verified against both CPSC notices (opened 2026-11-16). Both give the manufacture window as 1983 through 1994, so installed_from/installed_to stand. The '1983-1992' wording is not a conflict about manufacture: the 2001 notice's 'Sold At' line says the recalled private-label units were sold January 1983 through December 1992. Unit counts do differ between the two CPSC texts: about 190,000 in the September 2000 warning versus about 140,000 in the July 2001 recall notice (of which about 110,000 carried Premier/Consolidated labels and about 30,000 were private-label units covered by the recall). Fire reports: about 30 (2000) and 50 (2001).
entries.regions: California only (units built with NOx rods to meet California air-quality rules)
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: about 140,000 units (2001 notice) or about 190,000 (2000 warning), 50 fires reported, installed exclusively in California. No denominator of California homes built 1983-1994 was computed and no data exists on how many units survive 30+ years later; most are past normal furnace life, hence 'rare'.
entries.how_to_identify: Look at the furnace in the attic or crawlspace: steel rods mounted above the burners (the 'NOx rods') identify all of them. Brand labels include Consolidated, Premier, Addison and Weatherking (not covered by the 2001 recall programme) and private labels Amana, Bard, Sunburst/Carrier, Goettl, Goodman/GMC/Janitrol, Comfort-Aire, Trane and American Standard (CPSC lists the model numbers).

risk.safety: Fire: CPSC reported about 50 fires; no injuries cited in the recall notice. CPSC suggested an ionization smoke alarm in the attic as an interim measure.
risk.financial: No manufacturer remedy remains (firm bankrupt; litigation remedy expired). Owner pays for a new furnace.
risk.insurance_or_sale: A home inspector who recognises it will call for replacement; may be a negotiation item in a California sale.

fix.what: Replace the furnace.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

sources.supports: Recall 01-189 (9 July 2001): about 30,000 private-label furnaces recalled out of about 140,000 made for California 1983-1994; 50 fire reports, no injuries; NOx-rod identification; sold Jan 1983-Dec 1992; remedy no longer available

entries.name: Cadet / Encore in-wall electric fan heaters (recalled)
entries.summary: Small electric fan-forced heaters recessed into walls, very common in Pacific Northwest houses and apartments. CPSC sued Cadet in 1999 and a February 2000 settlement recalled more than 1.9 million units because they can overheat, spark and catch fire. The discounted-replacement programme ended on 17 February 2002, so recalled units still in walls should be replaced.
entries.date_notes: Corrected in the verification pass: installed_to changed from 1999 (trade press) to 2000, because the only CPSC text that gives years for the whole 1.9-million-unit recall (release 03-030, opened) says the heaters were sold and distributed 'from about 1978 through 2000'. The February 2000 recall notice itself gives no years. The 1997 CPSC notice for the first, 190,000-unit recall says those units were installed 1985 through 1992. Per-series dates from InspectAPedia (FW 1978-1989, FX and LX 1984-1995) and the trade-press 1982-1999 range were not verified. CPSC's wording is 'about', so treat both ends as approximate.
entries.regions: Mainly Washington, Oregon, California, Idaho, Montana (also Wyoming per the 1997 notice)
entries.prevalence_basis: 1.9 million units concentrated in about five states is a large number, but no source gives the share of homes; applies mostly to homes with electric zonal heat. No survival data.
entries.how_to_identify: Remove nothing: read the label on the front of the heater assembly behind the grille. Recalled models begin FW, FX, LX, TK, ZA, Z, RA, RK, RLX, RX, RW or ZC followed by three digits; brands Cadet and Encore.

risk.safety: Fire and burn hazard. CPSC's later reminder cited four deaths, two serious burn injuries and six partial or total house fires (three deaths and five fires in the February 2000 text).
risk.financial: Replacement of each heater at owner's cost now; several per house is typical.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Commonly flagged in Pacific Northwest home inspections.

fix.what: Replace each recalled heater with a current model.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Plexvent / Ultravent high-temperature plastic vent (HTPV) pipe on gas furnaces and boilers
entries.summary: Grey or black plastic vent pipe used to vent mid-efficiency gas or propane furnaces and boilers through a side wall. CPSC and the appliance makers announced a recall programme in 1998 because the pipe can crack or separate at joints and leak carbon monoxide into the house.
entries.date_notes: Verified: CPSC gives a year range only for one subset, about 10,000 systems on Goodman mid-efficiency furnaces manufactured October 1988 to July 1994, and installed_from/installed_to are those subset dates. None of the four CPSC releases opened states an installation window for all ~250,000 systems; my recollection of roughly 1987-1993 remains unconfirmed, so date_confidence stays low.
entries.regions: national (cold-climate states most likely)
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: about 250,000 systems nationally (1998 release); about 93,000 replaced as of 1 October 2005 (CPSC release of 7 Nov 2005). That is a small share of the housing stock and the attached appliances are now 30+ years old.
entries.how_to_identify: Follow the furnace or boiler flue: a grey or black plastic pipe going out through a side wall, printed 'Plexvent', 'Plexvent II' or 'Ultravent'. White PVC or CPVC pipe is not part of the recall.

risk.safety: Carbon monoxide poisoning from cracked or separated vent joints.
risk.financial: Under the 2009 revision, Plexvent owners were offered a free new vent or up to $400 rebate; Ultravent owners about $250. Whether any of this is still honoured is unknown.
risk.insurance_or_sale: A known inspection call-out; a CO hazard an inspector will report.

fix.what: Replace the vent system or, more realistically at this age, the appliance.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Gravity ('octopus') furnace with asbestos-wrapped ducts
entries.summary: A large basement furnace with no blower: warm air rises through big round ducts that branch out like octopus arms. Originally coal-fired and often converted to oil or gas, they are roughly 50% efficient and the furnace and ducts were typically insulated with asbestos. (Asbestos itself is covered in the hazmat domain.)
entries.date_notes: InterNACHI says only 'late 1800s to the mid-20th century'; no source gives firm start, end or peak years. 1880 and 1950 are placeholders for that phrase, not documented dates.
entries.regions: national, concentrated in cold-climate houses with basements (Midwest, Northeast)
entries.prevalence_basis: No survey data found on how many remain. Original presence in pre-1940 basement houses was common, but most have been replaced; 'rare' reflects survival today, not original installation.
entries.how_to_identify: Basement: a very large round or boxy furnace with multiple large sheet-metal ducts sloping upward from the top, no blower compartment, often white or grey cloth-like or corrugated-paper wrap on ducts (possible asbestos; do not disturb).

risk.safety: Asbestos fibre release if insulation is damaged or disturbed; combustion safety of a very old converted appliance.
risk.financial: High fuel bills (InterNACHI: only about half the heat reaches the house); removal needs asbestos abatement and usually new ductwork.
risk.insurance_or_sale: InterNACHI advises buyers to negotiate price to cover asbestos and furnace removal.

fix.what: Licensed asbestos abatement, then replace with a modern furnace and ducts.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

sources.supports: era (late 1800s to mid-20th century), only about half the heat is used, asbestos insulation, advice to negotiate price for removal
sources.quote: These antiquated furnaces were installed from the late 1800s to the mid-20th century and are still found in use in some older buildings.

entries.open_questions: Any dated end of production; survival rate; cost of abatement plus replacement.

verification.what_is_confirmed: InterNACHI (trade, opened): the era phrase 'late 1800s to the mid-20th century', the roughly-half efficiency statement, asbestos wrap and the buyer advice.
verification.what_is_not: No primary source. 1880 and 1950 remain placeholders for InterNACHI's phrase; no firm start, end or peak years, no survival data.

entries.name: Buried (underground) home heating oil tank
entries.summary: Bare steel tanks buried in the yard to hold heating oil. They corrode and leak, contaminating soil and groundwater, and the homeowner is generally responsible for cleanup. Many were abandoned in place when houses converted to gas, so a house can have one without having oil heat.
entries.date_notes: Still no source dates the era of residential installation; 1930-1985 remains my unverified general understanding. Verified in the second pass: EPA says that until the mid-1980s most underground tanks (of all kinds) were bare steel, which corrodes and leaks; that is consistent with, but does not establish, a mid-1980s end to bare-steel residential tanks. EPA also confirms heating-oil tanks used on the premises are excluded from the federal UST rules, so there is no national cut-off date. State service-life figures (Massachusetts 10-20 years, Maryland about 15, Idaho about 30) were seen only as search extracts; the state hosts are not on the allowed list.
entries.regions: Regional: Northeast and Mid-Atlantic (NJ, NY, CT, MA, PA, MD), plus Pacific Northwest and other oil-heat pockets
entries.prevalence_basis: No prevalence data found. Likelihood depends on whether the neighbourhood was ever on oil heat; cannot be stated from year built alone.
entries.how_to_identify: Outside: a fill pipe and a vent pipe near the foundation, or capped pipes; inside: cut-off copper oil lines through the basement wall. Absence of pipes does not prove absence of a tank; a tank sweep (metal detection or GPR) is the usual check.

risk.safety: Low direct safety risk; environmental contamination of soil and drinking-water wells.
risk.financial: A 2011 Philadelphia Inquirer report put simple removal at $1,500-$2,000, with cleanup of a leaked tank running into tens of thousands. NJDEP runs an Unregulated Heating Oil Tank programme; its grant fund has been reported as depleted.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Lenders and buyers in oil-heat regions often require removal or a clean tank test; state guidance (MD, MA) says replace any buried tank over about 15-20 years old or of unknown age with an above-ground tank.

fix.what: Tank sweep, then removal (or approved closure in place) with soil testing; remediate if leaked.
fix.cost_source: Philadelphia Inquirer, 21 Oct 2011, removal only, no leak (seen as search extract; dated; leak cleanup is far higher and unbounded)

entries.name: Air conditioner or heat pump that uses R-22 (Freon)
entries.summary: Central air conditioners and heat pumps made before 2010 use the ozone-depleting refrigerant HCFC-22 (R-22). US production and import of R-22 ended on 1 January 2020, so a leak now has to be topped up from recovered or stockpiled refrigerant, which is scarce and expensive. EPA does not require replacement, but any such unit is also at or past normal service life.
entries.date_notes: End date verified against EPA (three documents opened): from 1 January 2010 HCFC-22 could be produced or imported only for equipment manufactured before that date, and all production and import ended 1 January 2020. Not verified: the trade-press 'dry-charge' loophole (R-22 condensing units shipped without refrigerant and sold as replacements for some years after 2010), which would mean a post-2010 replacement unit can still be R-22. The 1960 start is a placeholder for when central AC became common; no source opened gives a start year. R-410A units were sold alongside R-22 for some years before 2010 (unverified).
entries.regions: national
entries.prevalence_basis: Applies only where the original (or a pre-2010 replacement) unit is still running. At a typical 10-15+ year life most pre-2010 units have been replaced, but no survey figure was found.
entries.how_to_identify: Read the data plate on the outdoor unit: 'R-22' or 'HCFC-22' (newer units say R-410A, or R-454B/R-32). The manufacture date is usually on the same plate.

risk.safety: None directly to occupants.
risk.financial: A refrigerant leak can make repair uneconomic; the indoor coil usually must be replaced with the outdoor unit when changing refrigerant.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Inspectors routinely note R-22 systems as near end of life; buyers may ask for a credit.

fix.what: Continue to run until it fails, then replace the system (outdoor unit and indoor coil).
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session. No current R-22 price per pound was found.

entries.name: Unlined or deteriorated masonry chimney
entries.summary: Older brick chimneys were often built with no clay tile liner, or have liner tiles that have cracked. Without a sound liner, heat, flue gases and acidic condensate attack the brick and mortar and can reach nearby wood framing. Current model codes (IRC R1003.11) require every masonry chimney to be lined.
entries.date_notes: I could not find a source that pins when liners became a code requirement. The Chimney Safety Institute of America says flue lining 'has been recommended since the early part of this century' (i.e. early 1900s) and cites National Bureau of Standards tests in the 1940s that called unlined chimneys 'little less than criminal'. A code-explainer site says homes built 'before the 1950s' often have unlined chimneys. Adoption was local and gradual; 1950 is an approximate end, not a code date. installed_from is null because chimneys predate any useful start year. Verification pass: the only reachable statement is Wikipedia's (secondary) 'Since the 1950s, building codes in many locations require newly built chimneys to have a flue liner', which agrees with the approximate 1950 end but is not a code citation. The CSIA page, the NBS report (nvlpubs.nist.gov) and the ICC code text are on hosts that were not allowed or refuse automated requests.
entries.regions: national
entries.prevalence_basis: No prevalence data found. Sources say only 'often' for pre-1950s houses. Separately, lined chimneys of any age can have cracked tiles, and an old oversized chimney serving a newer gas appliance can suffer condensation damage.
entries.how_to_identify: Look up from the fireplace or down from the clean-out with a torch: bare brick and mortar means unlined; square orange/buff clay tiles mean lined. Cracked tiles usually need a camera inspection (NFPA 211 Level 2).

risk.safety: Chimney fire spreading to framing; carbon monoxide leakage into the house.
risk.financial: Relining is a significant repair; not doing it can make the fireplace or appliance flue unusable.
risk.insurance_or_sale: A Level 2 chimney inspection is commonly recommended at sale; some insurers ask about wood-burning appliances.

fix.what: Install a listed stainless-steel liner or cast-in-place liner, or re-tile; or decommission the flue.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Yellow corrugated stainless steel gas tubing (CSST) without lightning bonding
entries.summary: Flexible yellow-jacketed stainless steel gas piping used in place of black iron pipe. A nearby lightning strike can arc through its thin wall and ignite the leaking gas. Since the 2009 model gas codes it must be directly bonded to the electrical grounding system with a 6 AWG copper conductor; earlier installations often are not.
entries.date_notes: Start: one source says NFPA 54 first approved CSST in the US in 1988; I use 1990 as the practical start of installation in houses (unverified; my assignment brief also mentions 1990). End of the 'unbonded' era: direct bonding became mandatory in the 2009 NFPA 54 (section 7.13.2) and, from memory, the 2009 IRC/IFGC, but states adopted those editions years later and manufacturers' instructions required bonding from about 2006-2007 after the class settlement. CSST itself is still installed today (installed_to marks the end of routinely unbonded installs, not of the product). Verification pass: neither the 1988/1990 start nor the 2009 code date could be checked, because no allowed government host carries them and codes.iccsafe.org refuses automated requests. InterNACHI (opened) words the class as CSST 'installed in homes as of September 5, 2006', which answers one open question at trade-source level.
entries.regions: national; lightning exposure highest in the Southeast, Gulf and Midwest
entries.prevalence_basis: No market-share figure was found this session. Applies only to houses with gas service.
entries.how_to_identify: Look at exposed gas piping in the basement, attic, crawlspace or at the furnace/water heater: a flexible corrugated tube in a yellow jacket (black jacket on newer arc-resistant products). Bonding is a clamp on a rigid gas fitting with a bare or green 6 AWG copper wire running to the electrical panel or grounding electrode.

risk.safety: House fire after a direct or nearby lightning strike.
risk.financial: Bonding is a small electrician job; a 2007 class settlement offered vouchers of $75-$160 toward a bonding jumper or $200-$2,000 toward a lightning protection system (claims closed 5 Sept 2007).
risk.insurance_or_sale: Many home inspectors flag unbonded yellow CSST as a standard report item.

fix.what: Have a licensed electrician bond the gas piping per the tubing manufacturer's instructions and current code.
fix.cost_source: Voucher values for a bonding jumper in the 2007 Arkansas class settlement, as reported by PM Magazine (search extract; a proxy, not a current market price)

entries.name: Old uncoated brass flexible gas appliance connector
entries.summary: The flexible corrugated tube joining a gas range, dryer or water heater to the gas pipe. Older connectors made of uncoated brass have soldered end fittings that can crack or separate, especially when the appliance is moved, causing gas leaks, fires and explosions. CPSC says any uncoated brass connector should be replaced.
entries.date_notes: Corrected in the verification pass. The CPSC release I had dated 1997 is release 97-003 dated 10 October 1996, and says uncoated brass connectors 'have not been made for at least the past 10 years', i.e. not since about 1986 at the latest. installed_to is therefore changed from 1980 (an undocumented midpoint) to 1986, the latest year the primary source allows; manufacture may have stopped earlier, and CPSC gives no actual year, so confidence stays low. Later wordings (CPSC publication 'more than 30 years', a gas-utility page 'more than 20') were not opened. No start year found.
entries.regions: national
entries.prevalence_basis: No count found. A connector is normally replaced with the appliance, so only homes with very old original gas appliances are likely to have one.
entries.how_to_identify: CPSC says do not move the appliance to look. If visible: a dull brass-coloured corrugated tube with no grey/yellow plastic coating; modern connectors are stainless steel or coated. Have a professional check.

risk.safety: Gas leak, fire or explosion. CPSC (Oct 1996): 200 reports of these connectors failing, associated with 35 deaths and 59 injuries.
risk.financial: Inexpensive part; the cost is the service call.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Routine inspection defect.

fix.what: Have a qualified person fit a new stainless-steel or plastic-coated connector; never reuse a connector.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Smoke alarms: missing, battery-only, not interconnected, or over 10 years old
entries.summary: What a house was built with depends on its year: none before the mid-1970s, a single hallway alarm after that, then hard-wired, then interconnected alarms in every bedroom with battery backup. Older houses are not automatically upgraded, and any alarm more than 10 years old should be replaced regardless.
entries.date_notes: Milestones seen this session, mostly from secondary sources that disagree: (a) 1973 - first required in a model code (ICBO Uniform Building Code, hallway outside bedrooms), with other model codes and the CABO One- and Two-Family Dwelling Code following 1975-76; NFPA 101 (1976) required them in homes. (b) Hard-wired in new construction - a home-inspector summary puts it at the 1979 UBC; Minnesota's state fire marshal page uses a 1989 cut-off for its own rules. (c) Every sleeping room and interconnection - one source says the BOCA/ICBO/SBCCI codes from 1988; a UBC summary says 1988 = every floor and 1991 = every sleeping room; NFPA 72 required bedrooms in 1993; a New Jersey municipality uses 1 May 1993 for hard-wired with battery backup in all bedrooms. So 'in bedrooms' is 1988-1993 depending on code family, plus local adoption lag. (d) Replace at 10 years - NFPA 72 from 1999 per one source. installed_to 1993 marks the last year a new house could plausibly have been built without bedroom alarms under a model code; local adoption could be later. Verification pass: no primary code text could be opened (codes.iccsafe.org refuses automated requests; the WPI, Minnesota, ICC press and other pages are on hosts not allowed). Wikipedia (secondary, opened) repeats the same chronology as the weak advocacy site: NFPA 101 in 1976, model codes requiring interconnection and all sleeping rooms from 1988, NFPA 74 interconnection in 1989, NFPA 72 bedrooms in 1993, ten-year replacement in 1999. The 1973 UBC first-requirement date and the hard-wiring date were not confirmed anywhere. NIST (primary) confirms only the research history and an adoption figure.
entries.regions: national; exact dates depend on which model code (UBC west, BOCA northeast/midwest, SBC south) and edition the state or city had adopted
entries.prevalence_basis: NIST (opened): the share of homes with at least one smoke alarm rose from 10% in 1975 to at least 92% by 2000, so having some alarm is near-universal; that figure says nothing about bedroom coverage, interconnection or age of the alarms. Otherwise reasoning, not data: any house built before the early 1990s was built to a lesser standard than today's and whether it has since been upgraded is unknown.
entries.how_to_identify: Count them: one in each bedroom, one outside each sleeping area, one per level including basement. Press test on one - if all sound, they are interconnected. A unit with no wiring behind it is battery-only. Check the manufacture date on the back; over 10 years means replace.

risk.safety: Late or no warning of fire, especially with bedroom doors closed.
risk.financial: Low: alarms are cheap; hard-wiring an older house costs more, and wireless-interconnect alarms are an alternative.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Many states and cities require working alarms (some require 10-year sealed-battery units, e.g. California, Illinois, Maryland per a manufacturer's compliance guide) at sale or rental.

fix.what: Add alarms to every bedroom, hallway and level; use interconnected (wired or wireless) units; replace any over 10 years old.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: No carbon monoxide alarms (houses built before CO alarm rules)
entries.summary: Carbon monoxide alarms were not part of model residential codes until the 2009 International Residential Code, which requires them in new homes that have fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage. Houses built before a state adopted that rule often have none unless a state law required a retrofit.
entries.date_notes: A trade article states the CO alarm requirement was added in the 2009 IRC (section R315, from memory); later editions (2018, 2021) keep the trigger 'fuel-burning appliance or attached garage'. I could not read the 2009 text. Many states had their own statutes before or after 2009 and adopted the 2009 IRC on different dates, so the practical cut-off varies by state from roughly the mid-2000s to the mid-2010s. Verification pass: the 2009 IRC date could NOT be confirmed. codes.iccsafe.org refuses automated requests, NCSL and the trade sites are not on the allowed list, and neither CPSC, EPA, HUD nor Wikipedia pages opened mention the IRC requirement. The only dated fact confirmed is one state example (Colorado law effective 1 July 2009, via Wikipedia).
entries.regions: national model code; state statutes vary (NCSL keeps the state list)
entries.prevalence_basis: Reasoning: any house built before its state's adoption was built without CO alarms. NCSL says most states now have some CO detector requirement, many applying at sale or rental. No data on actual presence.
entries.how_to_identify: Look outside each sleeping area and on each level for a unit labelled 'carbon monoxide' or a combination smoke/CO alarm. CO alarms expire (commonly 5-10 years; see the date on the unit).

risk.safety: CO poisoning from furnaces, water heaters, fireplaces, generators or cars in attached garages.
risk.financial: Low: plug-in or battery units.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Often required at sale or in rentals under state law.

fix.what: Install listed CO alarms outside each sleeping area and on every level.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Bedroom windows too small or too high to escape through
entries.summary: Modern codes require every bedroom (and habitable basement) to have a window or door big enough to climb out of and for a firefighter to enter. Houses built before these rules, and many basement bedrooms added later, have windows that are too small or too high off the floor.
entries.date_notes: Uniform Building Code history from city/state handouts: no requirement in early editions; 1964 UBC - 5.0 sq ft net opening, 24 in. by 24 in. minimum, sill max 48 in.; 1976 UBC - 5.7 sq ft, 24 in. min height, 20 in. min width, sill max 44 in., which is essentially today's IRC rule (5.0 sq ft allowed at grade floor). Local adoption lagged: Sacramento used the 1976 UBC from July 1977, Fort Collins from Dec 1977, Minnesota from Sept 1978 (with a 48 in. sill amendment). I found nothing for the BOCA or Southern codes, so dates outside UBC states are unknown. installed_to 1976 = the edition in which the modern dimensions appeared.
entries.regions: national; dates shown are for Uniform Building Code jurisdictions (mostly western and some midwestern states)
entries.prevalence_basis: No data. Pre-1964 houses had no rule; 1964-1976 houses met a slightly smaller rule. Basement bedrooms are the most common failure in any era.
entries.how_to_identify: Open the bedroom window fully and measure the clear opening: at least 24 in. high and 20 in. wide, 5.7 sq ft total (5.0 at ground floor), with the sill no more than 44 in. above the floor. Basement windows need a window well you can climb out of.

risk.safety: Occupants trapped in a bedroom fire; firefighters cannot enter.
risk.financial: Cutting in a basement egress window with a well is a substantial job.
risk.insurance_or_sale: A room without a compliant egress opening may not be countable as a bedroom in a listing or appraisal, depending on local rules.

fix.what: Enlarge the window / add an egress window and well; existing houses are generally not required to upgrade unless altering or adding a bedroom.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Garage door opener without auto-reverse / photo-eye sensors
entries.summary: Automatic garage door openers made before 1991 may not reverse when the closing door hits a person, and those made before 1993 lack the second safety system (photo-electric eyes or a sensing edge). Children have been killed by entrapment under closing doors.
entries.date_notes: Verified against CPSC and the CFR (opened 2026-11-16). The Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act of 1990 required openers manufactured on or after 1 January 1991 to meet UL 325's entrapment-protection requirements (reverse within two seconds of hitting a two-inch block); CPSC codified this in June 1991. Additional protection (an electric eye, a door-edge sensor, or a constant-contact wall button) applies to openers manufactured on or after 1 January 1993 (CPSC final rule announced 3 December 1992; 57 FR 60455, 21 Dec 1992). 16 CFR 1211.1 in the 2023 CFR reads 'January 1, 1993', so the 'January 21, 1993' seen in a search extract was an extraction error. Note that the 1993 rule can be met by a constant-contact button instead of photo-eyes, so a 1993+ opener without eyes is possible though uncommon. This is the opener's manufacture date, not the house's build date; openers are often added or replaced later.
entries.regions: national
entries.prevalence_basis: Typical opener life is 10-15 years (InterNACHI chart), so a pre-1993 opener still in service is unusual, but no survey figure was found.
entries.how_to_identify: Look for two small sensor 'eyes' about 6 in. off the floor on each side of the door opening; none means pre-1993 (or disabled). Check the date on the opener's label. Test: door should reverse on contact with a 2x4 laid flat on the floor.

risk.safety: Crushing or entrapment, mainly of children. CPSC (Dec 1992): reports of 54 children aged 2 to 14 killed since 1982 after becoming trapped under doors with automatic openers.
risk.financial: Cost of a new opener.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Routine home-inspection safety item.

fix.what: Replace the opener with a current UL 325-compliant unit; do not try to retrofit very old units.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Ordinary (non-tempered) glass in doors, sliding doors and shower enclosures
entries.summary: Before the federal safety glazing standard, patio doors, storm doors, glazed entry doors and tub/shower enclosures were often made with ordinary annealed glass, which breaks into large sharp shards. The CPSC standard (16 CFR Part 1201) applies to glazing made after 6 July 1977 for these products.
entries.date_notes: Verified against 16 CFR Part 1201 (2023 CFR via govinfo) and the 2016 Federal Register notice: 1201.7 sets the effective date as 6 July 1977 (rule published 6 January 1977, 42 FR 1427, amended 20 June 1977), with fire-door glazing delayed to 6 January 1980 and pre-1977 tempered glass allowed in products through 5 July 1981. The covered products are confirmed from 1201.1(a): storm or combination doors, doors, bathtub doors and enclosures, shower doors and enclosures, and sliding glass (patio-type) doors. Not verified: that many states had their own safety-glazing laws from the late 1960s and early 1970s (from memory). Building codes added further hazardous locations (glass near doors, floors, stairs, tubs) over later editions, so some locations in post-1977 houses can still be non-tempered.
entries.regions: national (federal rule); earlier state laws vary
entries.prevalence_basis: Reasoning: a pre-1977 house that still has its original sliding door, storm door or shower enclosure plausibly has annealed glass, particularly if built before the state's own glazing law. No survey data found.
entries.how_to_identify: Look in each corner of the glass for a small etched or sand-blasted 'bug' naming the maker and 'tempered' or '16 CFR 1201' / 'ANSI Z97.1'. No mark on a door or shower panel in an older house suggests ordinary glass (laminated safety glass also carries a mark).

risk.safety: Severe lacerations from falls into or through the glass.
risk.financial: Replacing a patio door or shower enclosure, or applying an approved safety film as a lesser measure.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Inspectors commonly note missing safety-glazing marks in hazardous locations.

fix.what: Replace with tempered or laminated safety glazing.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Stair and deck railings with wide gaps (pre-4-inch-sphere rule)
entries.summary: Current codes require guards (railings on stairs, balconies, decks) to be built so a 4-inch sphere cannot pass through, to stop small children slipping through. Older houses were built to 6-inch or even 9-inch spacing rules, or none.
entries.date_notes: I found no primary source. Building-official forum recollections: older model codes allowed 9 in., then 6 in. from the mid/late 1980s, then 4 in.; BOCA adopted the 4-inch sphere in its 1990 edition; the 1992 CABO One and Two Family Dwelling Code is quoted (section R-214.2) as 4 in. with 6 in. allowed at the stair tread/riser/bottom-rail triangle, though another poster recalls 1992 CABO as 6 in.; and 'many jurisdictions never followed the 4-inch sphere till the mid-90s'. From memory the UBC moved 9 in. -> 6 in. in 1985 and -> 4 in. in 1991, unconfirmed. Today's IRC: 4 in., with 4 3/8 in. on the open side of stairs and 6 in. at the stair triangle.
entries.regions: national; date depends on model code family and local adoption
entries.prevalence_basis: Reasoning: houses built before about 1990 with original railings were built to a wider rule. No survey data.
entries.how_to_identify: Measure the clear gap between balusters and under the bottom rail; anything over 4 in. (4 3/8 in. on stair sides) is below current standard. Also check guard height (36 in. minimum in current IRC).

risk.safety: Falls of small children through or under the guard.
risk.financial: Adding intermediate balusters or infill panels is usually modest; replacing a whole railing is more.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Frequently written up by home inspectors as a child-safety item; not normally a required retrofit.

fix.what: Add balusters, cable/mesh or panel infill, or replace the guard.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

entries.name: Home fire sprinklers (required by model code since 2009 IRC, rarely adopted)
entries.summary: The 2009 International Residential Code added a requirement for fire sprinklers in new one- and two-family homes from 1 January 2011 (townhouses earlier). Almost every state deleted the requirement when adopting the code, so most new houses still have none; California and Maryland (and Washington DC) are the notable exceptions.
entries.date_notes: Model-code date verified via NIST (primary, opened): the IRC change requiring sprinklers in all new one- and two-family homes became effective 1 January 2011 (the NIST abstract does not name the edition or section; '2009 IRC' and 'R313' remain from memory and the unopened ICC release). State adoption: Wikipedia (secondary, opened) says California and Pennsylvania were first in 2011 and Pennsylvania repealed the same year, which matches my recollection. Maryland and Washington DC as adopters, and the NAHB statement that almost all states removed the requirement, were not verified (hosts not allowed). Some cities have long required sprinklers locally. This is a 'present since' entry: installed_from is when a new house in an adopting state would have them.
entries.regions: California and Maryland statewide (new homes from 2011), Washington DC, plus scattered local ordinances
entries.prevalence_basis: Outside adopting jurisdictions, sprinklers in single-family houses are uncommon; within California and Maryland a house built from 2011 on should have them. No national percentage was found.
entries.how_to_identify: Small sprinkler heads (often under flat white cover plates) in ceilings of every room; a riser with a gauge and flow switch near the water main or in the garage.

risk.safety: Benefit, not hazard. Absence means no automatic suppression.
risk.financial: Systems need little maintenance but freeze damage and accidental discharge are possible; painted or obstructed heads must be replaced.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Some insurers discount for sprinklers.

fix.what: Not a retrofit most owners make; where present, keep the control valve open and heads unpainted.
fix.cost_source: No credible figure found this session.

feasibility_notes: Mixed. (1) Recalls and federal rules are highly feasible: CPSC notices and the CFR give exact dates, unit counts and identification marks (Consolidated furnaces 1983-1994, Cadet heaters, HTPV vent pipe, garage door openers 1 Jan 1991 / 1 Jan 1993, safety glazing 6 July 1977, R-22 1 Jan 2010 / 1 Jan 2020, sprinklers 1 Jan 2011). Even so, CPSC's own releases disagree with each other on year ranges and counts, so a second pass must read the notices, not summaries. (2) Building-code milestones are the hard part: smoke alarms, egress windows, baluster spacing and chimney liners changed edition by edition in three or four competing model codes (UBC, BOCA, SBC, CABO) and then took effect locally years later. Free online evidence is mostly municipal handouts (good, but UBC-only) and practitioner forum recollections (weak). A reliable product needs the legacy code books or ICC's archive, and should present these as 'model code year, your jurisdiction may be later' rather than a single year. Baluster spacing and chimney liners have the thinnest evidence; I could not pin a liner date at all. (3) Prevalence is almost never quantified: recalls give unit counts but no surviving population; code items have no survey of actual presence. Nearly all prevalence values here are reasoning, and say so. (4) Lifespans: EPA (septic) and DOE (water heater) give usable figures; furnace and AC are reasonably triangulated (InterNACHI, NYSERDA/DOE, contractor data); windows, electrical panels and well pumps have no authoritative figure I could find. The two obvious sources, InterNACHI's chart and the NAHB 2007 study, were visible only in fragments. (5) Costs: almost nothing credible; left null except EPA's septic range, a 2011 newspaper oil-tank figure and 2007 settlement voucher values. (6) The decisive limitation of this pass is that page fetching was blocked by the session network policy, so zero sources are verified. A second pass needs cpsc.gov, epa.gov, ecfr.gov, energy.gov, nachi.org, iccsafe.org, ncsl.org, nist.gov, govinfo.gov and state .gov hosts allowed, after which most of the recall/federal-rule entries could be verified in an hour.
